lessons.title: Determining Harvest Maturity
lessons.body:
Knowing when to harvest onions is critical for storage life and market quality. Onions are ready when the tops (leaves) begin to yellow, weaken, and fall over naturally. This usually happens 90 to 120 days after transplanting, depending on variety and climate. In Africa, where many farmers grow short-day varieties like Red Creole or Bombay Red, maturity can be as early as 80 days in hot lowlands. Do not wait until all leaves are brownâif the necks are still thick and green, the bulbs are not mature and will not store well.

A simple field test: dig up a few bulbs and check the neck. A mature onion has a thin, papery neck that is soft and dry. If the neck is thick and juicy, wait a few more days. Also, the skin should be tight and papery, and the bulb should feel firm. Another sign: the outer scales become dry and rustle when you rub them. In sandy soils, bulbs may push themselves partly out of the ground, making them easy to see.

Timing also depends on the weather. If rain is coming, harvest early to avoid rot. In dry areas like northern Nigeria or Senegal, let the tops dry completely in the field if no rain is expected. But in humid regions like Uganda or Cameroon, harvest as soon as 50% of the tops have fallen to prevent fungal diseases. Use a calendar and walk your field every 2-3 days as harvest approaches.

Do not harvest when the soil is wet; wet soil clings to bulbs and increases rot. If you must harvest after rain, lift bulbs and let them dry in a shaded, ventilated area before curing. Remember: over-mature onions may split or sprout in storage, while immature ones shrivel. Aim for 70-80% of tops fallen and dry. For seed production, wait until seed heads turn brown, but for bulb harvest, follow the leaf signs. A good rule: when you can pinch the neck and it feels like paper, it's time.

lessons.title: Harvesting Techniques: Lifting, Topping, and Windrowing
lessons.body:
Harvesting onions by hand is common in Africa, but proper technique prevents bruising and extends shelf life. Start by loosening the soil around the bulbs with a fork or hoe, then lift them gently by the neck or under the bulb. Never pull by the leavesâthey may tear, opening the bulb to rot. In large fields, you can use a plough or tractor-drawn lifter, but set it shallow to avoid cutting bulbs. Work in dry conditions, preferably in the morning after dew has dried.

After lifting, leave the onions in the field to dry for 2-3 days. This is called windrowing. Arrange them in rows with the tops of one row covering the bulbs of the next, so the bulbs are shaded from direct sun but still get air. In hot, dry areas like Egypt or Sudan, windrow for 3-5 days; in humid areas, only 1-2 days, then move to a shed. If rain threatens, cover windrows with tarps or move onions under shelter. The goal is to dry the outer skin and neck, not to cook the bulbs.

Topping (cutting the leaves) is done after drying. Leave about 2-3 cm of neck attached to the bulb. Cutting too close invites rot; leaving too much neck slows curing. Use sharp shears or a knife, and discard any bulbs with thick necks or signs of disease. In some regions, farmers braid the tops and hang them, but for bulk storage, topping is better. If you plan to store in sacks, topping is essential to reduce bulk and prevent sprouting.

Windrowing also helps synchronise maturity. After 2-3 days, the necks should be completely dry and the outer skin papery. If you see new roots emerging, the onions are re-growingâmove them to a dry, ventilated place immediately. Remember: every bruise is an entry point for rot. Handle bulbs like eggs. Use baskets or crates, not sacks that crush. In Kenya, farmers often use wooden crates for transport to avoid damage. After windrowing, gather onions in the cool of the evening to reduce heat stress.

lessons.title: Curing Onions for Storage
lessons.body:
Curing is the most important step for long-term onion storage. It dries the neck and outer scales, sealing the bulb against rot and sprouting. In Africa, where humidity can be high, curing must be done properly or you lose your harvest within weeks. There are two methods: field curing and artificial curing. Field curing works in dry areas with low rainfall. After windrowing, leave onions in the field for 2-3 weeks, turning them every few days. But if rain is likely, move them to a shaded, well-ventilated shed.

For artificial curing, spread onions in a single layer on racks or shelves in a dry, airy room. Aim for 25-30Â°C and relative humidity below 70%. Good airflow is keyâuse fans if available, or open windows and doors. In West Africa, some farmers use raised platforms under a thatched roof. Curing takes 2-4 weeks. The necks should be completely dry and papery, and the outer scales should rustle. When you cut a bulb, the neck should be tight and no moisture should appear.

During curing, check for rotten bulbs daily. Remove any soft, smelly, or sprouting onions immediatelyâthey release ethylene gas that speeds up spoilage of others. Also, protect from rain and direct sun. In humid regions like the Congo Basin, curing may take longer; consider using a solar dryer or a well-ventilated barn. A simple test: after 2 weeks, squeeze the neck of a few bulbs. If it's still green or damp, cure longer. If it's papery and dry, curing is done.

Once cured, onions can be stored for 3-6 months in cool, dry conditions. Without curing, they may last only 2-4 weeks. Curing also improves flavour and appearance. Do not wash onions before curingâmoisture encourages rot. If onions are muddy, let them dry, then brush off soil gently. After curing, move to storage. Remember: curing is not drying in the sun until they bake; it's a slow, ventilated drying process. In Ethiopia, farmers store cured onions in ventilated sacks in a dark room. Always keep cured onions off the floor on pallets to prevent moisture uptake.

lessons.title: Grading and Sorting for Market
lessons.body:
Grading and sorting onions increases your income because buyers pay more for uniform, high-quality bulbs. After curing, spread onions on a clean surface and remove any that are soft, bruised, diseased, or sprouting. Also remove bulbs with thick necks, doubles (two bulbs fused), or sunburn. These can be sold separately for processing or home use, but not for premium market. In Africa, many traders reject mixed sizes, so grading by size is essential.

Use simple tools: a wooden or plastic sizing ring, or just your hands. Common grades: large (over 6 cm diameter), medium (4-6 cm), and small (under 4 cm). In Kenya, large onions fetch up to 30% more than small ones. You can also grade by colourâred, yellow, or whiteâand by shape (round, flat). For export, stricter standards apply, but for local markets, consistent size and cleanliness matter most. Remove loose skins and trim necks to 1-2 cm.

Sorting also means separating onions for different uses. Firm, well-cured bulbs go for fresh market. Slightly blemished ones can be sold for processing (soups, sauces). Rotten ones must be destroyed or buried, not left in the field. In Nigeria, some farmers grade into three categories: Grade A (export), Grade B (urban supermarkets), Grade C (local markets). This increases overall returns.

Do grading in a shaded area to avoid sunscald. Use clean crates or baskets. Never mix grades in one containerâbuyers will pay the lowest price. Also, grade before storage if you plan to sell later, because re-grading after storage causes extra handling damage. A good practice: grade at harvest, then store in labelled crates. For small-scale farmers, grading by size can be done with a simple mesh screen. Remember: uniform onions in a bag look professional and attract repeat buyers. In Tanzania, women's groups often do collective grading to meet larger orders. Always wear gloves to protect bulbs from fingernail cuts.

lessons.title: Packaging and Storage Conditions
lessons.body:
Proper packaging and storage keep onions fresh and reduce losses. For storage, onions need cool temperatures (0-5Â°C is ideal, but in Africa, 10-15Â°C is more practical), low humidity (65-70%), and dark, ventilated conditions. In many African homes, a well-ventilated shed or room works. Avoid storing near fruits like bananas or tomatoesâthey release ethylene that makes onions sprout. Also, keep away from strong-smelling chemicals.

Packaging options: for short-term storage (1-2 months), use mesh bags or netted sacks that allow airflow. For longer storage, use ventilated crates or wooden boxes. Never use plastic bagsâthey trap moisture and cause rot. In West Africa, farmers often use jute sacks, but these absorb moisture; if used, keep them in a dry room. For transport to market, use rigid crates to prevent bruising. If you must use sacks, fill only halfway and do not stack heavy loads.

Stacking is important. Place crates on pallets 10-15 cm off the floor to allow air circulation and prevent moisture from the ground. Leave space between stacks for air movement. Do not stack more than 4-5 crates high, or the bottom ones will be crushed. Inspect stored onions every 2 weeks. Remove any sprouting or rotting bulbs immediately. A good storage room has vents near the floor and ceiling for natural convection.

For small quantities, you can hang braided onions in a cool, dry place. Braiding works best with long-necked varieties. For larger quantities, consider a simple evaporative cooling chamber (zero-energy cool chamber) made from bricks and sandâit can keep onions 5-10Â°C cooler than outside. In Kenya, such chambers reduce losses by 30%. Always label your storage with the date and variety. If you sell later when prices are high, proper storage pays off. Remember: onions are living bulbs; they respire. Good airflow is non-negotiable. In humid areas, use a dehumidifier if possible, or store only for short periods.

lessons.title: Reducing Post-Harvest Losses
lessons.body:
Post-harvest losses in onions can reach 30-50% in Africa, but simple steps can cut them to under 10%. The main causes are bruising, rot, sprouting, and weight loss. Start by harvesting at the right maturity, then handle gently. Every bruise becomes a rot entry point. Use padded baskets, avoid throwing onions, and never walk on them. In Nigeria, farmers who switched from sacks to plastic crates reduced losses by 25%.

Curing is your best defence. Proper curing reduces rot by up to 70%. After curing, store in cool, dry, ventilated conditions. Control temperature and humidity: if you see condensation on walls, increase ventilation. In humid regions, use charcoal or silica gel in storage rooms to absorb moisture. Also, remove diseased bulbs immediatelyâone rotten onion can spoil a whole crate. Check stored onions weekly and discard any soft or sprouting ones.

Sprouting is a major loss. To prevent it, store at low temperatures (below 10Â°C) or use sprout inhibitors like maleic hydrazide (approved in some countries). For organic farmers, keep storage dark and cool. Also, avoid excessive nitrogen fertiliser during growthâit makes bulbs sprout early. Harvest when 50-70% of tops fall; late harvest increases sprouting. In Ethiopia, farmers who harvest on time and cure well store onions for 5 months with less than 5% loss.

Transport losses are also high. Use crates, not sacks, and load carefully. Avoid long journeys in open trucks under hot sun. If you must transport far, do it at night or early morning. For market, sell in small lots to avoid repeated handling. Finally, keep records: note how much you harvest, store, and sell. This helps you identify where losses happen. In Ghana, a simple loss log helped farmers reduce waste by 15% in one season. Share tips with neighboursâcollective action improves everyone's storage. Remember: a little care after harvest doubles your profit.

quiz.q: What is the first sign that onions are ready to harvest?
options: A) The leaves turn completely brown
B) The tops begin to yellow and fall over
quiz.explanation: Onions are mature when the tops yellow and fall over naturally, not when they are completely brown.

quiz.q: How many days after transplanting do short-day onion varieties typically mature in hot lowlands?
quiz.explanation: Short-day varieties in hot lowlands can mature in about 80-100 days.

quiz.q: What is a simple field test to check onion maturity?
options: A) Cut the bulb and check for seeds
B) Squeeze the neck to see if it is dry and papery
C) Count the number of leaves
quiz.explanation: A dry, papery neck indicates maturity, while a thick, juicy neck means it is not ready.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid harvesting onions when the soil is wet?
options: A) Wet soil makes bulbs grow larger
B) Wet soil clings to bulbs and increases rot
C) Wet soil makes harvesting easier
quiz.explanation: Wet soil clings to bulbs, promoting fungal rot during storage.

quiz.q: What percentage of tops fallen is a good indicator for harvest?
quiz.explanation: Aim for 70-80% of tops fallen and dry for optimal maturity.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to lift onions from the soil?
options: A) Pull hard by the leaves
B) Loosen soil with a fork and lift gently by the neck or bulb
D) Use a spade to cut the roots
quiz.explanation: Loosening soil and lifting gently prevents bruising and neck damage.

quiz.q: What is windrowing?
options: A) Cutting the leaves before harvest
B) Arranging onions in rows with tops covering bulbs to dry
D) Storing onions in a shed
quiz.explanation: Windrowing is arranging onions in rows with tops shading bulbs for field drying.

quiz.q: How long should you windrow onions in a humid area?
quiz.explanation: In humid areas, windrow only 1-2 days to prevent fungal diseases.

quiz.q: When topping onions, how much neck should be left?
quiz.explanation: Leaving 2-3 cm of neck prevents rot and slows curing.

quiz.q: Why should you handle onions like eggs?
options: A) They are fragile and bruise easily
C) They need to be washed
quiz.explanation: Bruises become entry points for rot, so gentle handling is crucial.

quiz.q: What is curing?
options: B) Drying the neck and outer scales to seal the bulb
quiz.explanation: Curing dries the neck and outer scales, sealing the bulb against rot and sprouting.

quiz.q: What temperature range is ideal for artificial curing?
quiz.explanation: Curing is best at 25-30Â°C with low humidity and good airflow.

quiz.q: How long does artificial curing typically take?
quiz.explanation: Curing takes 2-4 weeks until necks are dry and papery.

quiz.q: What should you do with rotten onions during curing?
options: D) Bury them in the field
quiz.explanation: Rotten onions release ethylene and spread spoilage, so remove them at once.

quiz.q: How long can properly cured onions be stored?
quiz.explanation: Cured onions can store for 3-6 months under cool, dry conditions.

quiz.q: Why should you not wash onions before curing?
quiz.explanation: Washing introduces moisture that promotes fungal rot during curing.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of grading onions?
quiz.explanation: Grading allows you to sell uniform, high-quality bulbs at a higher price.

quiz.q: What size are large onions in diameter?
quiz.explanation: Large onions are typically over 6 cm in diameter.

quiz.q: How much more do large onions fetch compared to small ones in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Large onions can fetch up to 30% more than small ones.

quiz.q: Where should you do grading?
quiz.explanation: Grading in shade prevents sunscald and keeps onions cool.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity for onion storage?
quiz.explanation: Low humidity of 65-70% prevents rot and sprouting.

quiz.q: Why should onions not be stored near bananas?
options: B) Bananas release ethylene that makes onions sprout
D) Bananas make onions smell bad
quiz.explanation: Ethylene from bananas accelerates sprouting in onions.

quiz.q: What type of packaging is best for long-term onion storage?
quiz.explanation: Ventilated crates allow airflow and prevent moisture buildup.

quiz.q: How high should you stack onion crates?
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than 4-5 crates high can crush the bottom ones.

quiz.q: What is a zero-energy cool chamber?
options: B) An evaporative cooling chamber made of bricks and sand
quiz.explanation: It uses evaporation to keep onions 5-10Â°C cooler than outside.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of post-harvest losses in onions?
options: B) Bruising, rot, sprouting, and weight loss
quiz.explanation: These are the primary causes of post-harvest losses.

quiz.q: How can you reduce rot during storage?
quiz.explanation: Removing diseased bulbs prevents spread of rot.

quiz.q: What is a major cause of sprouting in storage?
options: B) High nitrogen fertiliser during growth
quiz.explanation: Excessive nitrogen makes bulbs sprout early.

quiz.q: When is the best time to transport onions to market?
quiz.explanation: Cooler times reduce heat stress and spoilage during transport.

quiz.q: What simple record-keeping practice can help reduce losses?
options: A) Noting harvest, storage, and sales
quiz.explanation: A loss log helps identify where losses occur and how to prevent them.
